steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on reconstructing the 3D scene an observer sees from images of their eyes, using NeRF. Open with an epigraph, explain the idea of eyes as mirrors, relate it to earlier corneal imaging work, describe the main challenges and how we address them, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
[quote: Proust on possessing other eyes]
1. The eye as a mirror: images of eyes contain the observer's world
2. Prior work on eye reflections; can we recover the world in 3D?
3. Our idea: 3D reconstruction from a sequence of eye images with NeRF
4. Challenges: source separation, cornea pose estimation
5. Our solution and evaluation
6. Contributions and broader impact

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
[quote: Proust on possessing other eyes]

1. Eye as mirror
- eye: remarkable organ, enables vision, holds information about surroundings
- own eyes: two lenses focusing light onto retina; looking at someone else's eyes we capture light reflected from cornea
- camera imaging another's eyes -> eyes become mirrors in the imaging system
- reflected light shares source with light reaching retina -> images contain info about world the observer sees

2. Prior work
- panoramic image of the observer's world from an image of two eyes
- follow-ups: personal identification, grasp posture, focused object estimation, relighting
- with advances in 3D vision/graphics: more than a single panoramic environment map or pattern recognition? full 3D?

3. Our approach
- reconstruct 3D scene from sequence of eye images
- insight: eyes capture/reflect multi-view info as heads move naturally
- classical imaging formulation + Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)
- standard NeRF: moving camera (+ pose estimation); ours: stationary camera, multi-view cues from eye images under head movement

4. Challenges
- conceptually simple, hard in practice
- source separation: reflections vs intricate iris textures; ambiguity; blended images break pixel correspondence
- cornea pose estimation: eyes small, hard to localize; reconstruction depends on locations and 3D orientations

5. Solution and evaluation
- repurpose NeRF for eye images: a) texture decomposition with simple radial prior; b) eye pose refinement
- synthetic dataset: complex indoor environment, synthetic cornea with realistic texture
- real-world setup with multiple objects
- extensive experiments on synthetic and real eye images to validate design choices

6. Contributions
- new 3D reconstruction problem: observer's world from eye images; foundational work + neural rendering
- radial prior for iris texture decomposition -> better radiance field
- cornea pose refinement for noisy eye pose estimates
- impact: neural rendering with partially corrupted observations from eye reflections; accidental imaging; 3D scenes beyond visible line-of-sight

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
- The only true voyage of discovery … would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another … – Marcel Proust, 1927

The human eye is a remarkable organ that lets us see, and it also holds valuable information about the world around us. Normally we use our own eyes as two lenses that focus light onto the photosensitive cells that make up our retina, but if we look at someone else's eyes we would also capture the light reflected from their cornea. When we use a camera to take images of another person's eyes, their eyes effectively become a set of mirrors in the whole imaging system. The light that reflects off the observer's eyes comes from the same source as the light that reaches their retina, so our camera should form images that contain information about the world that the observer sees.

Prior studies have looked at recovering a panoramic image of the world the observer sees from an image of two eyes. Follow-up works have explored applications like personal identification, detecting grasp posture, focused object estimation, and relighting. With the recent advancements in 3D vision and graphics, we wonder whether we can do more than reconstruct a single panoramic environment map or recognize patterns. Can we recover the world seen by the observer in full 3D?

In this paper we answer these questions by reconstructing a 3D scene from a sequence of eye images. Our starting insight is that our eyes capture/reflect multi-view information when we naturally move our heads. We take inspiration from the classical imaging formulation proposed by earlier work and combine it with the recent advances in 3D reconstruction led by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). The standard NeRF capture setup needs a moving camera to capture multi-view information (and often camera pose estimation after that), but our approach uses a stationary camera and gets the multi-view cues from eye images under head movement.

4. Challenges
- conceptually simple, extremely hard in practice
- source separation: reflections mixed with intricate iris textures; ambiguity; blended images disrupt pixel correspondence
- cornea pose estimation: eyes small, hard to localize; reconstruction depends on location and 3D orientation

5. Solution and evaluation
- repurpose NeRF: a) texture decomposition with radial prior; b) eye pose refinement
- synthetic dataset (indoor scene, synthetic cornea with realistic texture); real-world setup with multiple objects
- extensive experiments validating design choices

6. Contributions
- new 3D reconstruction problem
- radial prior for irises
- cornea pose refinement
- impact: corrupted observations from eye reflections; accidental imaging; beyond line-of-sight

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
- The only true voyage of discovery … would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another … – Marcel Proust, 1927

The human eye is a remarkable organ that lets us see, and it also holds valuable information about the world around us. Normally we use our own eyes as two lenses that focus light onto the photosensitive cells that make up our retina, but if we look at someone else's eyes we would also capture the light reflected from their cornea. When we use a camera to take images of another person's eyes, their eyes effectively become a set of mirrors in the whole imaging system. The light that reflects off the observer's eyes comes from the same source as the light that reaches their retina, so our camera should form images that contain information about the world that the observer sees.

Prior studies have looked at recovering a panoramic image of the world the observer sees from an image of two eyes. Follow-up works have explored applications like personal identification, detecting grasp posture, focused object estimation, and relighting. With the recent advancements in 3D vision and graphics, we wonder whether we can do more than reconstruct a single panoramic environment map or recognize patterns. Can we recover the world seen by the observer in full 3D?

In this paper we answer these questions by reconstructing a 3D scene from a sequence of eye images. Our starting insight is that our eyes capture/reflect multi-view information when we naturally move our heads. We take inspiration from the classical imaging formulation proposed by earlier work and combine it with the recent advances in 3D reconstruction led by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). The standard NeRF capture setup needs a moving camera to capture multi-view information (and often camera pose estimation after that), but our approach uses a stationary camera and gets the multi-view cues from eye images under head movement.

The idea is simple, but reconstructing a 3D NeRF from eye images is extremely hard in practice. The first challenge is source separation. We have to separate the reflections from the intricate iris textures of human eyes. These complex patterns add ambiguity to the 3D reconstruction. The eye images we get are inherently blended with iris textures, unlike the clear images of the scene that standard captures usually assume. This blending disrupts the pixel correspondence and makes the reconstruction harder. The second challenge is cornea pose estimation. Eyes are small and it is hard to localize them accurately from image observations. But the multi-view reconstruction depends on how accurate their locations and 3D orientations are.

To deal with these challenges, we repurpose NeRF for training on eye images by adding two crucial components: a) texture decomposition, which uses a simple radial prior to help separate the iris texture from the overall radiance field, and b) eye pose refinement, which makes the pose estimation more accurate even though eyes are small.

To evaluate how well our approach works, we generate a synthetic dataset of a complex indoor environment with images that capture the reflection from a synthetic cornea with realistic texture. We also build a real-world setup with multiple objects to capture eye images. We run extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world captured eye images to validate several design choices in our approach.

Our main contributions are:

- New 3D reconstruction problem. We present a new method for reconstructing 3D scenes of the observer's world from eye images, which combines earlier foundational work with the latest advancements in neural rendering.

- Radial prior for irises. We introduce a radial prior for iris texture decomposition in eye images, which improves the quality of the reconstructed radiance field a lot.

- Cornea pose refinement. We develop a cornea pose refinement procedure to reduce the noisy pose estimates of eyes, which handles the unique challenge of extracting features from human eyes.

These advancements extend what 3D scene reconstruction through neural rendering can currently do, so that it can handle partially corrupted image observations from eye reflections. This opens up new possibilities for research and development in the broader area of accidental imaging to reveal and capture 3D scenes beyond the visible line-of-sight.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
- The only true voyage of discovery … would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another … – Marcel Proust, 1927

The human eye is a remarkable organ that enables vision and holds valuable information about the surrounding world. While we typically use our own eyes as two lenses that focus light onto the photosensitive cells composing our retina, we would also capture the light reflected from the cornea if we looked at someone else's eyes. When we use a camera to image the eyes of another person, we effectively turn their eyes into a set of mirrors in the overall imaging system. Since the light reflecting off the observer's eyes shares the same source as the light reaching their retina, our camera should form images that contain information about the world the observer sees.

Prior studies have explored recovering a panoramic image of the world the observer sees from an image of two eyes [1,2]. Follow-up works have further explored applications such as personal identification [3,4], detecting grasp posture [5], focused object estimation [6], and relighting [7]. Given the recent advancements in 3D vision and graphics, we wonder: Can we do more than reconstruct a single panoramic environment map or recognize patterns? Is it possible to recover the world seen by the observer in full 3D?

In this paper, we answer these questions by reconstructing a 3D scene from a sequence of eye images. We start from the insight that our eyes capture/reflect multi-view information as we naturally move our heads. We draw inspiration from the classical imaging formulation proposed by [1] and integrate it with the recent advances in 3D reconstruction spearheaded by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [8]. Unlike the standard NeRF capture setup, which requires a moving camera to capture multi-view information (often followed by camera pose estimation), our approach uses a stationary camera and extracts the multi-view cues from eye images under head movement.

While conceptually straightforward, reconstructing a 3D NeRF from eye images is extremely challenging in practice. The first challenge is source separation: we need to separate the reflections from the intricate iris textures of human eyes. These complex patterns add a level of ambiguity to the 3D reconstruction process. Unlike the clear images of the scene typically assumed in standard captures, the eye images we obtain are inherently blended with iris textures, which disrupts the pixel correspondence and complicates reconstruction. The second challenge is cornea pose estimation. Eyes are small and hard to localize accurately from image observations, yet the multi-view reconstruction depends on the accuracy of their locations and 3D orientations.

To address these challenges, we repurpose NeRF for training on eye images by introducing two crucial components: a) texture decomposition, which leverages a simple radial prior to help separate the iris texture from the overall radiance field, and b) eye pose refinement, which improves the accuracy of pose estimation despite the small size of eyes.

To evaluate the performance and effectiveness of our approach, we generate a synthetic dataset of a complex indoor environment, with images capturing the reflection from a synthetic cornea with realistic texture. We further implement a real-world setup with multiple objects to capture eye images. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world captured eye images to validate several design choices in our approach.

Our primary contributions are as follows:

- New 3D reconstruction problem. We present a novel method for reconstructing 3D scenes of the observer's world from eye images, integrating earlier foundational work with the latest advancements in neural rendering.

- Radial prior for irises. We introduce a radial prior for iris texture decomposition in eye images, which significantly improves the quality of the reconstructed radiance field.

- Cornea pose refinement. We develop a cornea pose refinement procedure to alleviate noisy eye pose estimates, overcoming the unique challenge of extracting features from human eyes.

These advancements extend the current capabilities of 3D scene reconstruction through neural rendering to partially corrupted image observations obtained from eye reflections, opening up new possibilities for research in the broader area of accidental imaging [9,10,11,12] to reveal and capture 3D scenes beyond the visible line-of-sight.
